title: Deciphering Nociceptive Mechanisms: From Tissue Acidosis to Targeted Joint Pain Therapies
content: Chronic joint pain in arthropathies remains inadequately managed due to an overreliance on systemic therapies and incomplete models of peripheral nociception. Extracellular acidification is a hallmark of the pathological joint microenvironment, falling to pH 6.0–6.5 during ongoing inflammation, tissue ischemia, and cartilage breakdown. While rapid, transient proton-gated ion channels like ASICs and TRPV1 undergo rapid desensitization, persistent joint nociception is driven by non-desensitizing proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptors (PS-GPCRs). Specifically, activation of GPR65 on non-neuronal fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) triggers a Gs-cAMP-PKA signalling axis, prompting the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, CCL2) and lipid mediators such as sphingomyelin SM(d34:1) into the synovial fluid. This FLS-derived secretome directly lowers the rheobase and elevates action potential firing rates in primary knee-innervating dorsal root ganglion neurons, converting microenvironmental tissue acidosis into sustained sensory hyperexcitability. Traditional preclinical assessments relying on evoked reflex withdrawal fail to capture this unprovoked, ongoing pain, underscoring the utility of non-interventional ethological metrics, including spontaneous digging, burrowing, and 3D pose estimation. Bypassing systemic side effects through local intra-articular therapies such as TRPV1 antagonists, AAV-PHP.S-mediated chemogenetic silencing (hM4Di) of articular afferents, and mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs) effectively reverses primary afferent sensitization and rescues deficits in spontaneous ethological behaviour. Ultimately, targeting this stromal-neuronal FLS–GPR65 signalling nexus provides a novel, localized framework for non-opioid, disease-modifying joint pain therapeutics.
